rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to elute all 8 compounds if possible and map the overall elution window without being too compressed or too slow. This should reveal whether any peaks are unretained, missing by 42 min, or clustered in a specific phi range for later refinement.

All peaks elute within 4.1–9.4 min, corresponding roughly to phi_e about 0.21–0.45, so trim the gradient window around the actual elution region to increase selectivity and keep every peak inside the gradient. Holding tG and T constant isolates the effect of the narrower phi window on the unresolved 4/5 pair.

The narrow window improved the 4/5 pair but created a new 6/7 problem, so test pure slope sensitivity from the original broad method by doubling tG while keeping phi window and temperature fixed. If the critical pairs respond strongly, a shallower gradient may resolve them without needing a restrictive phi range.

The critical pair is strongly slope-responsive since tG 40 fully resolved everything but was too slow; estimate the shortest broad-window gradient likely to keep all pairs at or above 1.5 by stepping back toward the boundary from 40 min. A 24 min test should show whether full resolution can be retained while keeping t_last near 10 min.

The 4/5 pair improves mainly with shallower slope, but 24 min is still not enough; since the pair may also have temperature-sensitive selectivity, test a lower temperature at the faster 20 min broad gradient. This probes whether cooling can resolve the critical pair while keeping t_last close to the 10 min target.

At 25 C the troublesome pair is nearly resolved at tG 20, so make the smallest slope-softening change to try to push the 3/4 pair above R = 1.5. This directly targets full resolution with minimal added time, which should improve CRF if successful.

Since 20 min at 25 C is very close to optimal, probe whether a small temperature increase can shave retention time while preserving or slightly improving the near-critical 3/4 selectivity. This tests for a local optimum between 25 and 40 C without changing the slope.

The elution order around the critical cluster changes with temperature, indicating strong temperature-dependent selectivity there, so test 35 C to map that behavior between the poor 30 C and 40 C cases. This may reveal whether the optimum is sharply centered near 25 C or if another useful selectivity regime exists.

At the best condition, the first peak elutes relatively late, so raising phi0 slightly should shorten the run and may also shift selectivity within the crowded mid-gradient region while keeping all compounds in the gradient. This is a time-optimization test around the current best method without changing temperature or tG.

The current best is essentially optimal except the 3/4 pair is just below full credit, so make the smallest slope-softening change from that method to push it over R = 1.5. This is the most direct route to CRF 1.0 or very close to it.

The current best is limited only by a 0.03 min time penalty and a barely subcritical pair, so raise phi0 one more step to try to bring t_last just under 10 min while checking whether the 3/4 pair stays at or above its current near-threshold resolution. This is a direct time optimization around the best-known condition.

The last peak at the best method is right at 10 min, so slightly lowering phi1 may compress late retention just enough to remove the time penalty while preserving the favorable selectivity created by phi0 = 0.10 and 25 C. This explores time optimization via the upper end of the gradient rather than further increasing phi0, which hurt the critical 3/4 pair.

The best method at 20 min is already near ideal, so test a slightly steeper gradient to see whether the time gain can outweigh any small loss in the near-critical 3/4 resolution. This brackets the optimum in tG around the current best condition.

The critical cluster is highly temperature-sensitive and likely undergoes order changes, so test the same best phi window at 35 C to see whether the altered selectivity seen before can be made favorable with phi0 = 0.10. This is a targeted check for an alternative high-score regime not yet explored with the improved phi0.

At the best condition the critical 3/4 pair is just below full credit and all peaks elute inside the gradient, so narrow the upper end of the window while keeping phi0 and tG fixed to slightly flatten the effective slope in the occupied region. This may nudge 3/4 over R = 1.5 with only a small retention change.

We have not yet tested the best phi0 = 0.10 window at 40 C, and the temperature series shows strong selectivity changes in the critical cluster. This completes the temperature mapping around the best method and checks whether a different cluster becomes favorable enough to offset the faster run.

The best method is extremely close to full score, and the key question is whether a slightly longer gradient can achieve full resolution while only modestly increasing the time term. Testing 24 min from the best phi/T condition maps the local tradeoff beyond the 22 min point and helps confirm the true optimum.

With phi0 = 0.15 the run is safely under 10 min but the critical 3/4 pair only degrades slightly versus phi0 = 0.10, so one more step tests whether that pair remains near-threshold while gaining additional time margin. This helps confirm whether the true optimum in phi0 lies sharply at 0.10 or on a broader plateau.

Combine the two modest window changes that separately gave useful effects: higher phi0 cut time below 10 min, while lower phi1 improved resolution enough to clear all pairs. This tests whether their combination can preserve full resolution or near-full resolution while keeping t_last at or below 10 min.

Now that full resolution is achieved with time margin under 10 min, the only possible improvement is to shorten the method while keeping every pair at R >= 1.5. Reducing tG by one step is the cleanest test of whether the optimum can be made even faster without sacrificing the perfect CRF.

With a perfect method already found, the only remaining worthwhile exploration is whether a small temperature increase can further shorten retention while preserving full resolution in this improved phi window. This checks if the temperature sensitivity that hurt other windows might be benign or even favorable here.

The perfect method has some resolution margin, so reduce phi1 one more step at the same phi0, tG, and T to see if the run can be compressed while retaining all pairs above R = 1.5. This is the most plausible remaining way to keep CRF at 1.0 with a shorter analysis window.

The perfect method may tolerate a slightly higher phi0 because it has good resolution margin, and that could further shorten the run while keeping phi1 at the successful 0.90 value. This is the most informative remaining compression test near the optimum window.

A perfect CRF is already reached, but checking one step longer at the winning phi window will confirm whether 20 min is truly the shortest fully resolved setting or if there is extra robustness margin. This final local bracket around the optimum helps validate injection 19 as the best practical method.

Use the last injection to complete the local map around the winning phi1 = 0.90 window by testing the shorter 18 min gradient at lower phi0. This checks whether the faster method can be rescued by the more favorable phi0 = 0.10 selectivity, though injection 19 is already the benchmark winner.
